title: Fraudster jailed for using 10K bots and AI songs to outstream Taylor Swift
gist: Michael Smith was sentenced to 18 months and ordered to forfeit about $8.09 million for running bots to stream AI-generated songs across major platforms from 2017, the DOJ's first AI-assisted streaming fraud prosecution. His fake songs once out-streamed Taylor Swift's whole catalog 80.9 million to 9.3 million in a month.

insights.claim: Michael Smith used fake email accounts and fraudulently obtained debit cards to create thousands of accounts on Amazon Music, Apple Music, Spotify and YouTube Music starting in 2017, running bots to stream songs he claimed to own that the DOJ said were AI-generated.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Streaming platforms' account-verification was bypassable at scale for years.

insights.claim: By his 2024 arrest he had created hundreds of thousands of AI-generated songs and spread billions of streams across them so no single track raised red flags.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Dispersing plays over many tracks is the evasion technique detection systems must model.

insights.claim: In April 2023 Smith's fake songs were streamed 80.9 million times in one month versus 9.3 million for Taylor Swift's entire catalog.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Fraudulent volume dwarfed top real artists, showing how little scrutiny existed.
insights.locator: in a glaring example from April 2023

insights.claim: Smith was sentenced to 18 months in prison and must forfeit $8,091,843.64, in what the DOJ calls the first criminal case of AI-assisted streaming fraud in the US.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A precedent that AI-generated content fraud is prosecutable.

insights.claim: Because streaming royalties come from shared pools, fraudulent streams reduced payouts to genuine artists across the board.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Pro-rata royalty models make fraud a direct transfer from real artists.
insights.locator: Smith's streaming fraud didn't just hurt platforms

insights.claim: Smith's lawyers argued the DOJ should not punish one man for the 'ills of an industry', that he did not pocket $8 million, and that jail would delay repayment; the DOJ said he escalated deception, lied to police, and needed deterrence.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The defense signals industry-wide structural weaknesses; DOJ prioritizes deterrence.
